This page documents the **tract-level (area-level) environmental and sociodemographic
variables** in `class_data.csv`, converted from `Classdata_arealevelmeasures_description.docx`.
It's meant as a reference to check back to while working through the lessons — you don't need to
read it top to bottom.

::: {.callout-important}
## ⚠️ Please double-check before sharing with students

Two things in the source document are worth verifying against your original data-construction
code before this goes out:

1. **Traffic variable name.** The description below doesn't name a variable explicitly, but
   `class_data.csv` has a column called `ctb1traff` whose description ("average daily traffic,
   100 m kernel density, residential census tract") matches this section. I've assumed
   `ctb1traff` is the variable being described — please confirm.
2. **Education variable naming/direction.** The source document refers to `Educ_minHS` /
   `Educ_minBA` ("% persons **≥** high school" / "**≥** bachelor's"), but the actual columns in
   `class_data.csv` are named `Educ_ltHS` / `Educ_ltba` (**lt** usually means "less than," the
   opposite direction). I've labeled these with the `lt`-style names actually in the data, but
   the **direction of the percentage** needs your confirmation — is it "% with less than HS/BA"
   or "% with at least HS/BA"?
:::

## Traffic Volume

**Variable:** `ctb1traff`

Measured and estimated traffic volumes for major roads by road section are available annually
from PennDOT (2005–present). Air pollution levels from traffic typically return to background
levels within 100 to 300 m of roads. We calculated kernel densities of average daily traffic from
PennDOT traffic data within 100 m and 300 m of road centerlines, on a 30 m grid, for southeastern
Pennsylvania.

- 100 m was chosen based on work done for the New York City Community Air Survey.
- 300 m was chosen to account for the road width of wider roads.

The variable in the data set represents the **average of the 100 m kernel-density average daily
traffic** in the participant's residential census tract. **Higher value = greater traffic
volume.**

**Data sources**

- *Background:* Annual Average Daily Traffic by road segment, from the Pennsylvania Department of
  Transportation (PennDOT), Bureau of Planning and Research, Geographic Information Division.
- *Data obtained:* Downloaded from [www.pasda.psu.edu](http://www.pasda.psu.edu) (2005–2015
  downloaded 11/4/2016; 2016–2017 downloaded 4/26/2017).

## Land Cover: Tree Canopy & Grass/Shrub Cover

| Variable | Description |
|---|---|
| `hrlctree` | % of census tract area covered by tree canopy |
| `hrlcgrass_shrub` | % of census tract area covered by grass/shrub |

Derived from the Philadelphia Land Cover Raster, which provides data on surface types in
Philadelphia in 2008 and an update in 2018 (the 2015 value in this data set was created using
linear interpolation between the two). The data identifies seven categories: tree canopy,
grass/shrub, bare earth, water, buildings, roads, and other paved surfaces. When tree canopy
covers another surface type, that area is placed in the tree canopy category. Data were gathered
with the assistance of the University of Vermont Spatial Analysis Laboratory.

You can calculate a total vegetation measure by summing `hrlctree` and `hrlcgrass_shrub` together.

## Tract-Level Sociodemographic Composition

| Variable | Description | Interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| `race_blackNH` | % of tract population identifying as Black, non-Hispanic | Higher = greater % Black, non-Hispanic residents |
| `race_whiteNH` | % of tract population identifying as White, non-Hispanic | Higher = greater % White, non-Hispanic residents |
| `race_hisp` | % of tract population identifying as Hispanic/Latino | Higher = greater % Hispanic/Latino residents |
| `Educ_ltHS` | % of tract population, education attainment relative to high school (see note above — direction to be confirmed) | — |
| `Educ_ltba` | % of tract population, education attainment relative to bachelor's degree (see note above — direction to be confirmed) | — |
| `pov_allage` | % of tract population living in poverty (all ages) | Range 0–1; higher = greater % in poverty (0 = 0% in poverty; 1 = 100% in poverty) |
| `unemployed` | % of tract population unemployed (age 16+) | Higher = greater % unemployed |

**Data sources**

- *Background:* The American Community Survey (ACS), administered by the U.S. Census Bureau, is a
  nationwide survey providing social, economic, housing, and demographic data. The Census Bureau
  combines five consecutive years to produce estimates at the census tract level.
- *Data obtained:* ACS 5-year average data for 2017–2021, downloaded from the U.S. Census Bureau.
  Race/ethnicity variables were calculated as the percentage of persons in the census tract
  identifying with each category, across all age/gender groups. **Data may be missing** if a
  measure was suppressed by the Census Bureau due to low sample size (to protect against
  potentially identifying information).

## Crime Variables

Police-reported crime data is available from OpenDataPhilly. Yearly crime **rates** (per 10,000
persons) and **densities** (per square mile/km) for the City of Philadelphia were created for
calendar years 2006–2016. Crimes are categorized, with rates/densities available for violent
crime, narcotic drug violations, and property crime, summarized by 2010 U.S. Census Tract. These
rates were generated to provide objective measures of neighborhood safety, and can be used to
explore the influence of crime and safety on health outcomes and behaviors.

| Variable | Description | Interpretation | Missing data code |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ctviolra` | Rate per 10,000 population, violent crime | Higher = more crime | `9999999999` |
| `ctviolkm` | Density per sq. km, violent crime | Higher = more crime | `9999999999` |

::: {.callout-warning}
Note the missing-data sentinel value **`9999999999`** for the crime variables — this is *not* a
real crime rate. Be sure to recode it to `NA` before running any analysis or summary statistics
on `ctviolra`/`ctviolkm`, or it will badly distort means, ranges, and models.
:::

## Individual-Level Variables (Not Covered by This Codebook)

The variables below come from the participant-level survey rather than area-level environmental
data sources, and aren't described in `Classdata_arealevelmeasures_description.docx`. They're
listed here just so you know what's in `class_data.csv` and what still needs documentation:

`id`, `geoid10`, `year`, `age`, `gender`, `education`, `employment_status`, `race_ethnicity`,
`popden_km`, `stress`, `extreme_stress`, `physical_activity`, `current_smoker`, `obese`,
`self_reported_health`, `mental_health`, `improve_health`, `high_blood_pressure`, `diabetes`,
`daytime_safe`, `has_park`, `finds_fruits`, `grocery_access`, `social_capital`, `yes_adl`, `asthma`

::: {.callout-note}
If you have a separate data dictionary or survey instrument for these (e.g. from the original
study protocol), send it over and I can fold it into this page the same way.
:::
